Borrow vs Lend: The Ultimate Guide for Giving and Receiving

Introduction

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:01
Instaread

Do you ever freeze mid-sentence when you need to ask for a pen, or offer one to a friend? You are not alone. The verbs borrow and lend trip up even advanced English speakers because they depend on direction — who is giving, and who is receiving. This guide will make the difference crystal clear, help you avoid the most common ESL mistakes, and give you the confidence to use both verbs naturally in everyday conversations.

What Is Borrow vs Lend?

Simply put, lend means to give something to someone for a short time. The focus is on the person who provides the item. Borrow means to take something from someone for a short time. The focus is on the person who receives the item.

Think of it like a one-way street. If you are the giver, you lend. If you are the receiver, you borrow. You cannot do both with the same item at the same time. This direction is the core of the grammar.

Here is a quick mental shortcut: Lend starts with “L” for “Let someone have it.” Borrow starts with “B” for “Bring it to me.”

Rules

  1. Subject-Verb Agreement: The subject of the sentence determines the verb. If the subject is the person who gives, use lend. If the subject is the person who takes, use borrow.
  2. Preposition “to” after Lend: Use lend + something + to + someone. Example: “I lent my book to Maria.”
  3. Preposition “from” after Borrow: Use borrow + something + from + someone. Example: “I borrowed a book from Maria.”
  4. No Double Direction: You cannot say “borrow me” or “lend me from.” These are incorrect because they mix the two directions.
  5. Tense Changes: Lend is irregular: lend – lent – lent. Borrow is regular: borrow – borrowed – borrowed.
  6. Informal vs Formal: In British English, lend is common in daily speech. In American English, people often say “Can I borrow…?” or “Can you loan me…?” (loan is a noun but is used as a verb informally). Stick to lend and borrow for clarity in exams like IELTS or Cambridge.

How to Use It

Follow this simple three-step process to choose the correct verb every time.

Step 1: Identify Who Has the Item at the Start

Ask yourself: “Who owns the item right now?” The owner is the lender. The person who wants it is the borrower.

Step 2: Decide the Action from the Speaker’s View

If you are the owner, you lend. If you are the one who needs the item, you borrow. If you are talking about a third person, follow the same logic: the giver lends, the taker borrows.

Step 3: Choose the Correct Preposition

Use to after lend (direction goes away from you). Use from after borrow (direction comes toward you).

Example: “Could you lend your phone to me?” (You are asking the owner to give). “Can I borrow your phone from you?” (You are asking to take). Both are correct, but the first is more polite because it makes the listener the hero.

Examples in Sentences

  • Can you lend me your umbrella? It is raining outside.
  • I borrowed this novel from the library yesterday.
  • She lent her car to her brother for the weekend.
  • He borrowed money from his friend to buy lunch.
  • Could you lend a hand with these boxes? (idiom: help)
  • We borrowed the neighbour’s lawnmower last summer.
  • They lent us their tent for the camping trip.
  • I never lend my laptop to anyone – it has my work files.
  • She asked to borrow my notes for the exam.
  • He lent his jacket to the new student because she was cold.
  • You can borrow my charger, but please return it by 5 PM.
  • My dad lent me his tools to fix the bike.

Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: “Borrow me” instead of “Lend me”

❌ Wrong: “Can you borrow me your pencil?”

✅ Correct: “Can you lend me your pencil?” or “Can I borrow your pencil?”

Why: “Borrow” needs the receiver as the subject, not the giver.

Mistake 2: “Lend from” instead of “Borrow from”

❌ Wrong: “I lent some money from my sister.”

✅ Correct: “I borrowed some money from my sister.”

Why: “Lend” means give, so it cannot come “from” you.

Mistake 3: Forgetting the Irregular Past Tense of Lend

❌ Wrong: “She lend me her book last week.”

✅ Correct: “She lent me her book last week.”

Why: Lend is irregular; the past form is “lent.”

Mistake 4: Using “Borrow” for a Permanent Transfer

❌ Wrong: “I borrowed a gift for my friend’s birthday.” (Here it is a gift – you will not return it.)

✅ Correct: “I bought a gift for my friend’s birthday.” or “I borrowed a book for my friend’s birthday.” (only if you must return it)

Why: Borrow always implies returning the item.

Mistake 5: “Lend me from you” – Double Preposition

❌ Wrong: “Could you lend me your car from you?”

✅ Correct: “Could you lend me your car?” (no “from you” needed)

Why: The “to me” is already implied in the verb pattern.

Quick Summary

  • Lend = give (owner is the subject). Use “lend + something + to + someone.”
  • Borrow = take (receiver is the subject). Use “borrow + something + from + someone.”
  • Past tense: lend → lent, borrow → borrowed.
  • If you are asking for a favour, say “Could you lend me…?” or “Can I borrow…?” – both are polite.
  • Never say “borrow me” or “lend from.”

Practice Exercises

Fill in the blanks with the correct form of borrow or lend.

  1. Could you ______ me your phone for a quick call?
  2. I ______ this dress from my roommate for the wedding.
  3. He ______ his bicycle to his neighbour yesterday.
  4. She never ______ her books to anyone because they are precious.
  5. We need to ______ a projector from the office for the presentation.

Answers:

  1. lend (or “lend to me”)
  2. borrowed
  3. lent
  4. lends
  5. borrow

Check your answers: If you wrote “lend” in #1, you are asking the owner to give. If you wrote “borrow” in #2, you are the receiver. Great job!

Conclusion

Mastering borrow and lend is all about remembering one idea: direction. The giver lends, the receiver borrows. Practice by describing your daily life – who lent you what, and what did you borrow? With a little repetition, these verbs will feel natural, and you will never mix them up again.

FAQ

Q1: Is “loan” the same as “lend”?

Yes and no. Loan is a noun (a thing that is lent) and can be a verb in American English. However, lend is more formal and universally accepted in both British and American English. For example, “Can you loan me $10?” is fine in the US, but “Can you lend me $10?” is correct everywhere. In writing tests, always prefer lend.

Q2: Can I say “borrow to” someone?

No. Borrow always uses from because the direction is toward the speaker. “Borrow to” is incorrect. If you want to express giving, switch to lend with “to.”

Q3: What is the difference between “lend me” and “borrow me”?

“Lend me” is correct when you are the receiver asking the giver. “Borrow me” is wrong because it implies the giver takes something from you. Instead say, “Can I borrow it from you?”

Q4: How can I remember which verb to use in a fast conversation?

Use this mental trick: point your finger away from you when you say lend (giving away). Point your hand toward your chest when you say borrow (taking in). If you are unsure, rephrase: “Could I use your pen for a second?” This avoids the issue entirely, but for natural English, practice the lend/borrow pair out loud every day for a week.
